sections.b:
Isaiah 24–27 is often called the "Isaiah Apocalypse" because it widens the prophet's oracles against single nations into a judgment on the whole earth. The earth is emptied and reels like a drunk, a curse eats it because its people have broken "the everlasting covenant" (Isaiah 24:5), and the LORD judges "the army on high" and "the kings of the earth" and locks them in a pit (Isaiah 24:21–22). Then come a feast for all peoples, the swallowing of death (Isaiah 25:6–8), the rising of the dead (Isaiah 26:19), the slaying of Leviathan (Isaiah 27:1) and a great trumpet that gathers the scattered (Isaiah 27:13).

These chapters lack the visions, angel guides and numbered periods of Daniel or Revelation, so many scholars call them "proto-apocalyptic," a step toward the later genre. Their date is debated: from Isaiah's own day in the 700s BC to the Persian or even Hellenistic period. Revelation draws heavily on their imagery.
sections.refs: Isaiah 24:1–27:13; Isaiah 24:5; Isaiah 24:21–23; Isaiah 25:6–8; Isaiah 26:19; Isaiah 27:1; Isaiah 27:13; Daniel 12:2; Revelation 20:1–3

common: Isaiah 24–27 is an early form of the apocalyptic hope later found in Daniel and Revelation.
uncommon: Some conservative scholars hold that Isaiah of Jerusalem wrote these chapters in the 700s BC, and that their world-wide scope is prophecy rather than a sign of late date.

sections.b:
Two verses in Isaiah 24–27 are central to the Bible's hope of resurrection. Isaiah 25:8 promises that God "will swallow death up for all time," the verse Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 15:54. Isaiah 26:19 answers a community's lament: "Your dead will live! My corpses will stand up! Wake up and sing out, you who lie in the dust!" It is set against 26:14, where the dead oppressors "do not rise." Daniel 12:2 seems to build on its language of those who sleep in the dust waking up.

Readers have debated whether 26:19 promises bodily resurrection or pictures the revival of a crushed nation, as in Ezekiel 37. The Talmud cites it as proof of resurrection from the Prophets (Bavli Sanhedrin 90b), and the Targum reads "you revive the dead." Christian readers from the second century on have read it of the resurrection of the body.
sections.refs: Isaiah 25:8; Isaiah 26:14; Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2; Ezekiel 37:1–14; 1 Corinthians 15:54

common: Isaiah 26:19 is one of the earliest clear statements of resurrection hope in the Hebrew Bible.
uncommon: Some scholars read Isaiah 26:19 only as a metaphor for national restoration, with personal resurrection belief arising later.

sections.h: Leviathan and Rahab in Isaiah 27:1 and 30:7
sections.b:
Isaiah 27:1 promises that "on that day" the LORD will take his great sword to "Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the crooked serpent," and kill "the dragon that lives in the sea." The titles match almost word for word the monster Litan in the Ugaritic Baal texts (KTU 1.5 i 1–3; KTU 1.3 iii 38–42). Isaiah moves the ancient battle into the future: every power hostile to God will be judged. The Targum and Rashi read the monsters as empires (Egypt, Assyria and others), and Revelation identifies the dragon as "that ancient serpent called the Devil and Satan" (Revelation 12:9).

In Isaiah 30:7, the prophet mocks Egypt as "Rahab, who just sits there": the old sea monster's name, used for Egypt in Psalm 87:4, now describes an ally that roars but does nothing.
sections.refs: Isaiah 27:1; Isaiah 30:7; Isaiah 51:9; Job 26:12–13; Psalm 74:13–14; Psalm 87:4; Revelation 12:9

common: The language of Isaiah 27:1 draws on older Canaanite poetry about a sea monster.
uncommon: Some readers hold that the shared vocabulary reflects common poetic language rather than any borrowing of myth.

sections.b:
The fullest Old Testament picture of the end-time banquet is Isaiah 25:6–8. On "this mountain," Zion, where the LORD has just begun to reign (Isaiah 24:23), he spreads "a feast for all the peoples": rich food and aged wine strained clear. He swallows the face-cloth of mourning that covers the nations, swallows death itself, and wipes the tears from every face. The guest list is universal, and the meal is a coronation feast, like the meal of Israel's elders before God on Sinai (Exodus 24:11).

The Targum reverses it into a feast of judgment on the nations. Later Jewish tradition connected the banquet with Leviathan (Bavli Bava Batra 75a). Jesus' saying about many coming from east and west to eat with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matthew 8:11) and Revelation's "wedding supper of the Lamb" (Revelation 19:9) draw on this hope.
sections.refs: Isaiah 24:23; Isaiah 25:6–9; Exodus 24:11; Matthew 8:11; Revelation 19:9; Revelation 21:4

common: Isaiah 25:6–8 is the root of the later Jewish and Christian hope of a banquet in the kingdom of God.
uncommon: The Targum reads the feast as a cup of judgment for the nations rather than a celebration.

sections.b:
Against the rulers of Jerusalem, who boasted of a "covenant with death" (Isaiah 28:15), God lays in Zion "a stone that has been tested, a cornerstone of great worth," with the inscription-like promise, "Whoever believes will not hurry" (Isaiah 28:16). In Isaiah's day the stone was most likely God's promise to Zion and David's house, calling for trust instead of a panicked alliance with Egypt.

The Targum reads it as a king appointed in Zion, and the Qumran Community Rule applied it to the community's council (1QS VIII, 7–8). The Greek's "will not be put to shame" is the form quoted in Romans 9:33, Romans 10:11 and 1 Peter 2:6, where the stone is Christ, joined with the stumbling stone of Isaiah 8:14 and the rejected stone of Psalm 118:22.
sections.refs: Isaiah 28:15–17; Isaiah 8:14; Psalm 118:22; Romans 9:33; Romans 10:11; 1 Peter 2:6–8

common: The New Testament reads the stone of Isaiah 28:16 as Christ.
uncommon: Some interpreters read the stone as faith itself, or as the faithful remnant in Zion.

sections.b:
Isaiah 28–31 is the Bible's sharpest attack on foreign alliances. During Hezekiah's revolt against Assyria (705–701 BC), Judah's leaders sent envoys and treasure to Egypt (Isaiah 30:1–7; 31:1). Isaiah calls their treaty "a covenant with death" and "a lie" (Isaiah 28:15), accuses them of hiding their plans from God (Isaiah 29:15) and of going down to Egypt without asking for God's word (Isaiah 30:2). Egypt is "Rahab, who just sits there" (Isaiah 30:7).

Isaiah's alternative is trust: "By turning back and resting you will be saved; in calm and in trust your strength will lie" (Isaiah 30:15). His stance continued his advice to Ahaz a generation earlier (Isaiah 7:4, 7:9) and was echoed by Jeremiah and Ezekiel against later Egyptian alliances.
sections.refs: Isaiah 28:14–22; Isaiah 29:15; Isaiah 30:1–7; Isaiah 30:15–16; Isaiah 31:1–3; Isaiah 7:4–9; Jeremiah 2:18; Ezekiel 17:15

common: Isaiah's "covenant with death" is his name for Judah's treaty with Egypt against Assyria.

sections.h: Egypt in Isaiah 30: the useless helper
sections.b: In Isaiah 30 Egypt is the power Judah trusts in place of God. Judah's officials reach Zoan (Tanis) and Hanes (Herakleopolis) to secure the help of the Kushite pharaohs of the 25th Dynasty (Isaiah 30:4), and caravans carry treasure across the Negev "to a people that cannot do them any good" (Isaiah 30:6). Isaiah calls Egypt "Rahab, who just sits there" (Isaiah 30:7), the old sea monster with no bite. The irony runs back to the Exodus: Israel once came out of Egypt through the wilderness, and now Judah pays to go back, against the law that forbade returning to Egypt for horses (Deuteronomy 17:16). In 701 BC Sennacherib defeated the Egyptian army at Eltekeh.
sections.refs: Isaiah 30:1–7; Isaiah 31:1–3; Isaiah 19:11–13; Isaiah 36:6; Deuteronomy 17:16; Isaiah 27:13

sections.b: In Isaiah 28–30 Assyria is both God's instrument and God's target. It is the "someone strong and powerful" who will sweep away Samaria like hail and flood (Isaiah 28:2), the "flooding whip" that tramples Jerusalem's false shelter (Isaiah 28:18), and the speakers of the foreign tongue God will use to address his people (Isaiah 28:11). Yet the besiegers of Ariel vanish "suddenly, in a moment" (Isaiah 29:5–8), and in Isaiah 30:27–33 the LORD's name comes in fire: "At the voice of the LORD Assyria will be shattered" (Isaiah 30:31), and Topheth's fire pit is ready for its king. The rod of God's anger (Isaiah 10:5) is itself struck with the rod. Many readers connect these passages with Sennacherib's withdrawal from Jerusalem in 701 BC (Isaiah 37:36).
sections.refs: Isaiah 28:2; Isaiah 28:11; Isaiah 28:18; Isaiah 29:5–8; Isaiah 30:27–33; Isaiah 10:5; Isaiah 37:36; Isaiah 27:13

sections.h: The second song of the vineyard (Isaiah 27:2–6)
sections.b: Isaiah 27:2–6 answers the vineyard song of Isaiah 5:1–7. There the vineyard produced stinking grapes and God left it to thornbush and bramble. Here God sings over "a delightful vineyard": he waters it "moment by moment," guards it night and day, has "no fury" left, and would fight only the weeds that threaten it, unless they make peace with him. The song ends with Israel taking root and filling "the surface of the world with fruit" (Isaiah 27:6). The reversal shows that judgment was not God's final word for his vine. Jesus' "I am the real vine" (John 15:1) takes up the same tradition.
sections.refs: Isaiah 27:2–6; Isaiah 5:1–7; Psalm 80:8–16; Jeremiah 2:21; John 15:1–8

sections.b: Isaiah 27:13 promises that "a great ram's horn will be blown," and the lost in Assyria and the outcasts in Egypt will come and worship on the holy mountain in Jerusalem. The great shofar of ingathering became a central Jewish hope: the daily Amidah prays, "Sound the great shofar for our freedom," and the verse is read among the shofar verses of the Rosh Hashanah service. Jesus speaks of the Son of Man sending his angels "with a great trumpet" to gather his chosen (Matthew 24:31), and Paul of the trumpet at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16).
sections.refs: Isaiah 27:13; Isaiah 18:3; Leviticus 25:9; Zechariah 9:14; Matthew 24:31; 1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16

sections.b: Isaiah 27:12–13 pictures God beating out his harvest from the Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt and gleaning Israel "one by one," while a great shofar calls home "the strays perishing in the land of Assyria." Since Assyria deported the northern tribes in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6), many readers have heard a promise for the ten tribes. The Talmud cites the verse in its debate over whether the ten tribes will return (Bavli Sanhedrin 110b). Isaiah 11:11–16 makes a similar promise of a second exodus from Assyria and Egypt.
sections.refs: Isaiah 27:12–13; Isaiah 11:11–16; 2 Kings 17:6; Jeremiah 31:7–10; Ezekiel 37:15–22

sections.h: A pact with Sheol (Isaiah 28:15–18) and the shades (Isaiah 26:14, 19)
sections.b: Two passages in Isaiah 24–30 use the language of the underworld. In Isaiah 26:14 the dead oppressors are "shades" (refa'im) who "do not rise," but in Isaiah 26:19 the earth gives birth to its shades, God's own dead. In Isaiah 28:15 Jerusalem's rulers boast, "We have cut a covenant with death; with Sheol we have signed a pact." Isaiah is mocking their treaty with Egypt, and perhaps also hinting at cults of the dead (compare Isaiah 8:19; 29:4). God answers that their pact with Sheol "will not stand" (Isaiah 28:18).
sections.refs: Isaiah 26:14; Isaiah 26:19; Isaiah 28:15; Isaiah 28:18; Isaiah 8:19; Isaiah 29:4; Isaiah 14:9

sections.b: Isaiah 28:11 warns the mocking leaders of Jerusalem that God will speak to them "with jabbering lips and a strange tongue," the speech of Assyrian invaders, because they refused the plain message of rest (Isaiah 28:12). Paul quotes the verse in 1 Corinthians 14:21, in wording close to Aquila's Greek, to argue that tongues are "a sign for unbelievers" and that prophecy builds up the church better. The passage has become a key text in debates over whether tongues continue today: Pentecostals see a promise of Spirit-given speech, while many cessationists read Paul as treating tongues as a sign of judgment on unbelief.
sections.refs: Isaiah 28:11–13; Deuteronomy 28:49; 1 Corinthians 14:21–25; Acts 2:4–11

sections.b: Isaiah twice sums up God's offer to Judah as rest. In Isaiah 28:12 God had told them, "This is where rest is; give the tired ones rest," but they refused to hear. In Isaiah 30:15 the offer is repeated: "By turning back and resting you will be saved; in calm and in trust your strength will lie." Again: "But you refused." The rest is the security God promised Israel in the land (Deuteronomy 12:9), received by trust rather than by alliances and horses. The theme returns in Jesus' invitation, "I myself will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28), and in Hebrews 3–4.
sections.refs: Isaiah 28:12; Isaiah 30:15; Deuteronomy 12:9; Psalm 95:11; Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:1–11

sections.b: In Isaiah 24:13 the survivors of the world's judgment are like the few olives left after the tree is beaten and the last grapes after the harvest. In Isaiah 28:5, after the woe on Samaria's fading crown, "the LORD of Armies himself will be a crown of beauty and a wreath of splendor for the remnant of his people." In Isaiah 28:22 the decree of "an end, a settled end" repeats Isaiah 10:22–23, where only a remnant returns. The remnant theme in these chapters holds judgment and hope together.
sections.refs: Isaiah 24:6; Isaiah 24:13; Isaiah 28:5–6; Isaiah 28:22; Isaiah 10:20–23; Isaiah 27:6

sections.b: Isaiah 29:9–10 commands, "Blind your eyes and stay blind!" and says that the LORD has poured "a spirit of deep sleep" over the prophets. The whole vision becomes like a sealed scroll that no one can read (Isaiah 29:11–12), and the word of God becomes to the mockers the very nonsense they scorned, "so that they will go and trip backward" (Isaiah 28:13). These passages continue the commission of Isaiah 6:9–10. Paul joins the Greek of Isaiah 29:10 ("a spirit of stupor") with Deuteronomy 29:4 in Romans 11:8 to explain Israel's partial hardening, which he sees as temporary.
sections.refs: Isaiah 29:9–14; Isaiah 28:13; Isaiah 6:9–10; Deuteronomy 29:4; Romans 11:7–8; Romans 11:25–27

sections.h: Shut the door; the night of the festival (Isaiah 26:20; 30:29)
sections.b: Two passages in Isaiah 24–30 echo Passover night. In Isaiah 26:20 God's people are told, "go into your inner rooms and close your door after you," and hide until the fury has passed, as Israel stayed indoors while the LORD passed through Egypt (Exodus 12:22–23). In Isaiah 30:29 Judah's song at Assyria's fall will be "like the night when a festival is made holy," most likely Passover, "a night of keeping watch for the LORD" (Exodus 12:42). The people who sought refuge in Egypt will celebrate rescue as their ancestors did when they came out of it.
sections.refs: Isaiah 26:20–21; Isaiah 30:29; Exodus 12:22–23; Exodus 12:42; Isaiah 37:36

sections.b: Isaiah 30:33 announces that "Topheth was laid out long ago; it too has been made ready for the king." Topheth, in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, was where children were burned for Molech (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). The phrase "for the king" (lammelekh) is probably a pun on Molech's name. The king of Assyria will be the victim in the fire pit, lit by the breath of the LORD "like a stream of sulfur." The valley's name, Ge-Hinnom, later became "Gehenna," the place of final judgment.
sections.refs: Isaiah 30:33; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31–32; Jeremiah 19:6; Isaiah 66:24; Mark 9:43–48

sections.h: Tears wiped away and sevenfold light (Isaiah 25:8; 30:26)
sections.b: Isaiah 24–30 contains several pictures that later writers used for the new creation. God "will wipe the tears off every face" (Isaiah 25:8), a line Revelation repeats for the new heaven and earth (Revelation 21:4). Zion "will not weep, no, never weep again" (Isaiah 30:19). Lebanon turns into garden land (Isaiah 29:17), streams run on every hill, and "the sun's light will be seven times as strong" on the day God heals his people (Isaiah 30:25–26). The Talmud read Isaiah 30:26 of the days of the Messiah (Bavli Sanhedrin 91b), and Revelation goes further: the new Jerusalem needs no sun at all (Revelation 21:23).
sections.refs: Isaiah 25:8; Isaiah 29:17; Isaiah 30:19; Isaiah 30:23–26; Isaiah 60:19–20; Isaiah 65:17–19; Revelation 21:4; Revelation 21:23

sections.b: In the middle of the promise of a feast for all peoples, Isaiah 25:10–12 singles out Moab: it will be trodden down "the way straw is trodden down in the water of a manure pit" (Isaiah 25:10), its pride brought low and its high walls knocked to the dust. The word for manure pit, madmenah, may play on the Moabite town Madmen (Jeremiah 48:2). Many scholars think Moab here stands for the proud nations in general, as Edom does in Isaiah 34 and 63; others hear a real grievance, perhaps Moab's gloating over Jerusalem's fall (Ezekiel 25:8–11).
sections.refs: Isaiah 25:10–12; Isaiah 15:1–16:14; Jeremiah 48:1–47; Ezekiel 25:8–11; Zephaniah 2:8–11

sections.b: Isaiah 28:1–4 is a woe on "the crown that Ephraim's drunkards are so proud of," Samaria on its hill above a fertile valley. The garland of fading flowers worn at the leaders' drinking parties becomes a picture of the city itself, which Assyria will gulp down like the first fig of summer. The oracle comes from before Samaria's fall in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:5–6) and stands as a warning to Jerusalem, whose priests and prophets "too sway from wine" (Isaiah 28:7).
sections.refs: Isaiah 28:1–7; 1 Kings 16:24; Amos 6:1–6; 2 Kings 17:5–6

sections.b: The phrase "on that day" runs through Isaiah 24–30 like a refrain (Isaiah 24:21; 25:9; 26:1; 27:1; 27:2; 27:12; 27:13; 28:5; 29:18; 30:23). It introduces both judgment and salvation: the LORD calls the powers to account (Isaiah 24:21), kills Leviathan (Isaiah 27:1), gathers Israel (Isaiah 27:12–13), becomes a crown for the remnant (Isaiah 28:5) and opens deaf ears (Isaiah 29:18). "The day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall" (Isaiah 30:25) is also the day the LORD heals his people.
sections.refs: Isaiah 24:21–23; Isaiah 25:9; Isaiah 26:1; Isaiah 27:1–13; Isaiah 28:5; Isaiah 29:18; Isaiah 30:25–26; Isaiah 2:12–17

sections.h: God as the fortress of the poor (Isaiah 25:4; 26:6; 29:19)
sections.b: Isaiah 24–30 repeatedly sets the poor against the "brutal" ('aritsim). God has been "a fortress for the poor, a fortress for the needy in their trouble" (Isaiah 25:4). The proud town is trampled by "the feet of the afflicted, the tread of the poor" (Isaiah 26:6). When the brutal vanish and corrupt courts end, "the lowly will find more and more joy in the LORD, and the poorest of humankind will celebrate in the Holy One of Israel" (Isaiah 29:19–21).
sections.refs: Isaiah 25:4–5; Isaiah 26:5–6; Isaiah 29:19–21; Isaiah 3:14–15; Isaiah 11:4; Psalm 9:9

sections.b: Isaiah 24:21–22 says that the LORD will call to account "the army on high" and "the kings of the earth," who will be "locked in a dungeon, and after many days they will be called to account." Then the LORD reigns on Mount Zion. Many premillennial interpreters read the prison and the "many days" as the binding of Satan and the thousand years of Revelation 20:1–7; amillennial readers see a picture of final judgment without an earthly interval.
sections.refs: Isaiah 24:21–23; Revelation 20:1–7; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6

common: Isaiah 24:21–22 is one of the Old Testament passages behind the imprisonment of evil powers in Revelation 20.

sections.b: In Isaiah 27:9 Jacob's guilt will be atoned for when he grinds the stones of pagan altars to powder like chalk and leaves no Asherah poles or incense stands standing. In Isaiah 30:22 the restored people will treat their silver-plated and gold-covered idols as unclean and throw them out like a stained menstrual cloth, saying "Out!" In both, turning from idols is the visible sign of turning back to God.
sections.refs: Isaiah 27:9; Isaiah 30:22; Isaiah 2:20; Isaiah 31:7; Exodus 32:20; Deuteronomy 7:5; 2 Kings 23:4–15
